strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight: the initial seed noise strongly determines the structure of the final generation, and prior training-free inpainting methods neglect this; the paper builds a simple, effective optimization scheme on top of this observation.

Practical linearization of the denoising trajectory (Eq. 2-3) avoids back-propagation through the denoiser, making the method computationally feasible (~1 min/image, comparable to FLAIR at 50 NFE), which is an important engineering contribution.

Comprehensive evaluation across three standard benchmarks (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with multiple mask types, strong margins on LPIPS/FID/SSIM, and a well-designed ablation (Tab. 4) that substantiates each design choice (spectral vs. spatial optimization, gradient masking, latent-space nearest-neighbor fill).

The paper is honest about metric limitations (e.g., PSNR being misleading for inpainting) and discusses a concurrent work (FlowOpt) fairly, delineating the differences (spectral vs. spatial optimization, no inversion step).

Useful implementation insights (masking gradient updates to stay on the initial-noise manifold, purely latent-space operation with nearest-neighbor fills) with supporting visual evidence (Figs. 3, 5, 6).
Limitations and future work are discussed, and code release is promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single backbone (Stable Diffusion 3.5 medium) and a single downstream inpainter (BLD-SD3.5); the generality of the linearization across models, samplers, and NFE budgets is not demonstrated, weakening the claim of a general-purpose technique.

Fairness of the quantitative comparison is partially compromised: baselines are generated at native resolutions (512-768) and upsampled to 1024 for evaluation, while the method operates at 1024; baselines are also run both at their suggested NFE and 400 NFE, but the method's effective compute per iteration (one denoiser call per Adam step, ~20-40 iterations plus optimization overhead) is not clearly equated, making cross-method runtime/quality trade-offs hard to verify.

The core algorithmic novelty is modest and closely aligned with concurrent work (FlowOpt [35]) - the linearized update essentially drops the Jacobian, and the spectral-domain optimization, while empirically effective, is a small change without theoretical grounding for why it stabilizes optimization in this setting.

Prompts for FFHQ/DIV2K are generated by a VLM (Claude) from the masked image; this couples prompt quality to knowledge of the unmasked context and may systematically favor methods that reconstruct the ground-truth structure (as the method does by design). The sensitivity of results to prompt quality is not analyzed, and no human user study is conducted to corroborate the simulated preference metrics.

The method still relies on a downstream inpainter (BLD) after optimization; the interplay between optimized noise and the inpainter's own conditioning, and whether the gains transfer to other inpainting pipelines, is not explored.

Several hyperparameters (learning rate 3.0, T=20, number of iterations) are stated but their sensitivity is not ablated; the 'manifold of acceptable initial seed noises' motivating gradient masking is asserted empirically rather than characterized.

On BrushBench, the method is only third-best on IR/HPS v2/AS and trails BrushNet on several metrics; the narrative that LPIPS/FID are the 'right' metrics, while reasonable, is used to downplay unfavorable results without human validation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: the paper identifies the initial seed noise as an underexplored lever for training-free inpainting, supported by recent evidence that initial noise determines image layout, and demonstrates this convincingly (Fig. 2).

Two technically sensible contributions that make the idea practical: (i) a linearized approximation of the denoising trajectory that avoids back-propagating through the denoiser, and (ii) spectral-domain parameterization of the noise, both of which are ablated and shown to be critical (Tab. 4, Figs. 5-6).

Strong empirical evidence: consistent gains over both training-free (BLD, FLAIR, FlowChef, FlowDPS) and trained (BrushNet) baselines on three standard benchmarks (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench), with large margins on LPIPS and FID, plus extensive qualitative comparisons including 15 randomly drawn samples per dataset in the supplementary.

Honest metric discussion: the paper acknowledges the limitations of PSNR, CLIP, and preference metrics for inpainting and explains why LPIPS/FID are the most informative, rather than cherry-picking silently.

Practical details are disclosed (nearest-neighbor latent fill, gradient masking, Adam settings, NFE comparison), and code release is promised; runtime is reported and comparable to FLAIR despite 400 NFE.
Limitations and concurrent work (FlowOpt) are discussed transparently, with an empirical comparison against the spatial-domain variant of the concurrent approach.
weaknesses: The linearization is essentially equivalent to dropping the Jacobian, as the authors themselves note regarding concurrent FlowOpt; the theoretical justification for why this surrogate remains valid over 20 optimization steps is empirical only, and no analysis of approximation error or convergence is provided.

Evaluation fairness concerns: baselines are run at native resolutions (512-768) and resized to 1024 for evaluation while the proposed method operates natively at 1024x1024 with SD3.5, which may disadvantage competing methods; the heavy reliance on LPIPS/FID while down-weighting PSNR/CLIP (where the method loses to some baselines) should be scrutinized.

Prompts for FFHQ and DIV2K are generated by a commercial VLM instructed to describe the 'fully restored scene' including inferring content of the masked region, which is an unusual evaluation protocol; this gives all methods prompts that partially encode the ground-truth content and introduces a possible bias that is not analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to prompt quality).

The method is demonstrated only with one backbone (SD3.5 medium) and one downstream inpainter (BLD-SD3.5); generality across model families (e.g., UNet-based diffusion, other flow models) is unverified.

Several components are heuristic (learning rate 3.0, gradient masking, nearest-neighbor fill, fixed T=20), and robustness to these hyperparameters across mask types and datasets is not fully explored; the ablation is limited to FFHQ.

Per-image optimization (~1 minute on an RTX 5090) limits applicability to batch/large-scale settings; a more careful wall-clock comparison against baselines at matched quality would strengthen the claim of practicality.
No human study; conclusions about 'human preference' rest entirely on proxy metrics (IR, HPSv2, AS) that the authors themselves acknowledge are imperfect.

strengths: The core idea — optimizing the initial seed noise rather than the denoising trajectory — is well-motivated and clearly positioned against both guidance-based training-free methods and trained inpainting models, with convincing motivation (Fig. 2) that initial noise determines scene structure.

The two technical enablers (linearized trajectory approximation avoiding back-propagation through the denoiser, and spectral-domain optimization) are simple, practical, and well-supported: the ablation (Tab. 4) shows both gradient masking and spectral optimization are critical, and Figs. 3, 5, 6 provide intuitive visual evidence for why each component matters.

Experimental evaluation is thorough: three standard datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with different mask types, six baselines including a strong trained method (BrushNet) and the recent state-of-the-art FLAIR at both suggested and matched NFEs, and a broad suite of metrics. The method outperforms baselines on SSIM, LPIPS, and FID, the metrics most aligned with structural consistency.

The paper is unusually honest and careful in its metric discussion — correctly warning against over-reliance on PSNR/CLIP/IR/HPS v2 for inpainting — and the ablation comparing nearest-neighbor latent fills against ground-truth encoding is a nice touch that justifies a practical simplification.

The paper situates itself well w.r.t. concurrent work (FlowOpt), clearly articulating the differences (spectral vs. spatial optimization, no inversion initialization requirement) and empirically justifying them.

Appropriate attribution throughout, clear method presentation with a useful overview figure, and a stated commitment to code release; limitations and future directions (extension to other inverse problems) are discussed.
weaknesses: The linear approximation (Eq. 2) is largely heuristic. There is no theoretical or quantitative analysis of approximation error across trajectories, masks, or CFG scales; the claim that flow trajectories are 'approximately linear' is asserted rather than measured (e.g., no comparison against exact gradient unrolling on cases where it is feasible, even at fewer steps).

The spectral-domain optimization and the gradient masking trick are empirically motivated fixes for optimization instabilities, but the underlying failure modes are not deeply analyzed (e.g., is spectral whitening equivalent to per-frequency learning-rate scaling? would explicit per-frequency LR schedules in the spatial domain work as well?). This limits general insight and transfer to other inverse problems.

Cost and fairness of comparison deserve more scrutiny: the method effectively uses ~400 NFE-equivalent compute plus ~20 optimization iterations per image (~1 minute on an RTX 5090), and baselines are evaluated at their native resolutions (512–768) then resized to 1024 while the method operates natively at 1024; this asymmetry could favor the proposed method, and a resolution-controlled comparison or FLOP-matched table would strengthen the claims.

Results are somewhat mixed outside the favored metrics (third-best on IR/HPS v2/AS for BrushBench; lower PSNR/CLIP than some baselines), and the argument that LPIPS/FID are 'most important' is reasonable but self-serving; an actual human preference study would meaningfully strengthen the evaluation.

The formulation is claimed to generalize to other inverse problems (super-resolution, deblurring, video), but no experiments support this; the contribution remains confined to inpainting with a specific pipeline (optimized noise + BLD-SD3.5), so the dependence of the final quality on the downstream inpainter is not isolated (e.g., optimized noise + FLAIR, or optimized noise + plain sampling).

Some aspects lack clarity: how the masked-pixel gradient masking is exactly implemented in the spectral domain, sensitivity to learning rate and number of optimization iterations (only one example configuration is shown), and behavior under very large or irregular masks are under-explored; failure cases of the proposed method are not shown.

The method requires a diffusion/flow backbone with a well-conditioned latent space and its robustness rests on empirical observations (nearest-neighbor fill sufficiency); a VAE with different characteristics might not behave as well, which is not discussed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: optimizing the initial noise sample of a generic text-to-image flow model so that its denoised output is consistent with the unmasked region, then using it with a conventional training-free inpainter (BLD). This attacks a real and previously under-addressed failure mode (structural inconsistency between inpainted content and the target image), supported by a convincing motivating analysis (Figs. 2, 3, 9).

The combination of straight-through linearization of the denoising trajectory (Eq. 3-4), spectral-domain optimization with Adam as a per-frequency preconditioner, and gradient masking in unobserved regions is technically sound, practical (no back-prop through the denoiser, ~1 min/image, no carefully tuned learning rate or inversion initialization), and each design choice is empirically ablated (Tabs. 4, 9; Fig. 5-6, 10-12).

Extensive evaluation: three datasets with different mask types, six baselines plus extra comparisons against noise-optimization methods (InitNo, GoldenNoise, FreeInpaint) and a trained ControlNet inpainter, consistent gains in SSIM, LPIPS, and FID, and a reasonably designed 2AFC user study (N=37, 1,665 comparisons, 90% win rate with CIs).

The supplementary theoretical analysis (F.1) correctly identifies that spectral Adam is not equivalent to spatial Adam under coordinate-wise nonlinear preconditioners, giving real justification (beyond empiricism) for the spectral choice; generalization to non-flow backbones (SD1.5, SDXL) and video models supports broader applicability.
Honest metric discussion (PSNR/CLIP caveats), wall-clock and memory comparisons, and reproducibility aids (exact prompts, protocol details, project website).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental and partially concurrent-overlapping: the linearized objective (Eq. 3) is explicitly acknowledged to be the same straight-through estimator arrived at by concurrent work [49], so the core remaining novelty is spectral preconditioning (Adam in the Fourier domain) plus the spatial constraining heuristic—effective engineering, but modest algorithmic depth.

The spectral argument leans heavily on claims about frequency-dependent gradient variance in the latent landscape (F.2) that are asserted rather than measured directly; the theory is qualitative and the empirical evidence, while consistent, is confined to one backbone and inversion-style tasks.

Method is slower than most baselines (67s vs 4-22s) and yields lower PSNR on FFHQ/DIV2K than FLAIR; while the authors argue PSNR is a poor inpainting metric (defensible), the evaluation leans on LPIPS/FID as the decisive metrics with some selectivity (e.g., BrushBench FID 48 is high in absolute terms for all methods).

Only StableDiffusion 3.5 'medium' at 1024x1024 is evaluated in the main results for flow models; robustness across flow backbones, resolutions, and mask statistics (e.g., free-form/large masks beyond FLAIR's fixed patterns) is not systematically shown in the main text.

Presentation quality issues: several equations in the main text (Eqs. 1, 2, 3, 4) are rendered as raw LaTeX source, Fig. 4's caption block appears machine-generated/malformed, and the T-axis in Fig. 9 (values 1000→150) is inconsistent with the stated T=20, which hurts clarity and suggests insufficient proofreading.

Mask-type coverage is modest: FFHQ (fixed rectangle) and DIV2K (six rectangles) are simplistic; results on only one dataset (BrushBench) test segmentation-style masks, and BrushBench was created by the BrushNet authors, introducing a slight asymmetry in dataset provenance.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly motivates an underexplored angle for training-free inpainting: optimizing the initial noise sample so that unmasked structure is reproduced before running a conventional inpainting pipeline. Fig. 2 provides convincing evidence that the initial noise determines final structure, motivating the approach well.

The method is simple, practical, and well-motivated: linearization (dropping the Jacobian via a stop-gradient) avoids backpropagation through the denoising chain, and spectral preconditioning (Adam in the Fourier domain) stabilizes convergence. The empirical and theoretical analyses (Fig. 5, Sec. F) are careful—the non-equivalence proof for spectral vs. spatial Adam is correct in spirit and the argument that low/high frequencies have different gradient variances is plausible and well supported.

Evaluation is thorough: three datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with different mask types, consistent backbone across training-free baselines, comparisons against both trained methods (BrushNet, SD3 ControlNet) and noise-optimization baselines (InitNo, GoldenNoise, FreeInpaint), wall-clock/memory reporting, an ablation covering each design choice (spectral preconditioning, spatial constraining, nearest-neighbor fill vs. ground truth), and a reasonably sized 2AFC user study (N=37, 1,665 comparisons) with per-baseline win rates and confidence intervals.

The paper is refreshingly honest about metric limitations (e.g., PSNR and CLIP score caveats), and the theoretical upper-bound experiment showing nearest-neighbor filling matches ground-truth encoding is a useful robustness check. Limitations and future work are discussed.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the linearization is essentially the straight-through estimator / Jacobian-drop that appears in FlowChef, DiNG, and the concurrent FlowOpt [49]; the spatial gradient masking is a standard constraint. The genuinely new ingredient reduces to 'run Adam on the Fourier representation of the initial noise.' This is effective but thin as a core contribution, and the paper leans heavily on beating the concurrent work rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Possible metric circularity: the method directly optimizes masked reconstruction error, and the paper prioritizes SSIM/LPIPS/FID as the 'most important' metrics—metrics that reward exactly what the method optimizes (structural/perceptual fidelity to the observed content). The user study partially mitigates this, but the metric-selection argument should be treated with caution, and the authors' dismissal of PSNR/CLIP where they underperform deserves more scrutiny.

Practicality concerns are underplayed: per-image optimization (~67 s on an RTX 5090, 19.5 GB memory) makes the method far slower than trained methods (BrushNet at 5 s) and adds meaningful cost relative to simple pipelines; the 'training-free' framing does not fully acknowledge that it trades training cost for inference cost. Broader applicability beyond inpainting (super-resolution, deblurring) is only asserted or left as preliminary supplementary material.

The comparison with the concurrent FlowOpt [49] is deferred and only qualitative/descriptive; a direct head-to-head quantitative comparison on the same benchmarks would substantially strengthen the central claim that spectral preconditioning (rather than the shared Jacobian drop) is the decisive factor.

Evaluation uses one backbone family (SD 3.5 medium) for the main results; results on other backbones (SD1.5, SDXL) in the supplementary are limited to comparisons against noise-optimization baselines only, leaving the generality of the headline gains somewhat uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically relevant problem: making off-the-shelf text-to-image flow models effective for inpainting without task-specific training, and convincingly identifies the initial noise sample as the under-explored ingredient.

The method is simple, practical, and well-motivated: linearizing the denoising trajectory via a stop-gradient (recovering the straight-through estimator) avoids costly back-propagation through the denoising chain, and spectral preconditioning (Adam in the Fourier domain) with gradient masking on unobserved regions yields stable optimization in only ~20 iterations.

The empirical evaluation is thorough and above average: three standard datasets with different mask types (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench), many training-free and trained baselines run under a fair, shared backbone setup (SD3.5 medium), additional comparisons against noise-optimization methods (InitNo, GoldenNoise, FreeInpaint) and a trained ControlNet baseline in the supplement, a 2AFC user study (N=37, statistically significant gains), and wall-clock/memory reporting.

The ablations (Tab. 4, Fig. 5-6) are well-designed and directly support each design choice: spectral vs. spatial optimization with matched learning rates, spatial constraining, and the nearest-neighbor fill-in strategy (validated against the ground-truth upper bound).

The supplementary theoretical analysis (Sec. F) rigorously explains why spectral Adam is genuinely different from spatial Adam (non-commutativity of the Fourier transform with the coordinate-wise preconditioner), grounding the empirical convergence findings.

The writing is refreshingly candid about the relationship to prior work: the paper openly acknowledges that Eq. (3) is the straight-through estimator and that a concurrent work [49] arrives at the same objective, positioning its contribution on the preconditioning and constraint components; limitations and future work (other inverse problems, video inpainting) are discussed.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate: the linearized objective is explicitly the straight-through estimator, and spectral-domain optimization with Adam is a known technique; the contribution is best characterized as a careful systematization and stabilization of noise-space optimization for inpainting rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The case rests heavily on the empirical evidence that the combination matters.

The method still relies on an existing training-free inpainter (BLD) applied on top of the optimized noise; the paper does not evaluate the optimized-noise idea on top of other inpainting backbones (e.g., FLAIR, FlowChef) in the main text, so it is unclear how much of the gain is specific to the BLD pairing versus a general 'good initial noise' effect.

Results on metrics other than the favored ones (LPIPS/FID/SSIM) are mixed — PSNR and CLIP are often worse than baselines. The authors argue LPIPS and FID are the most meaningful metrics, which is defensible but somewhat self-serving; the argument would be stronger with more direct perceptual validation beyond the user study, which uses only 45 scenes.

The linearization assumption is validated empirically for SD3.5 flow trajectories (supplementary Fig. 9) but is known to degrade for non-rectified diffusion models; the non-flow experiments (SD1.5, SDXL) are qualitative with small gains, so generality across model families remains partially demonstrated.

The empirical comparison of convergence (Fig. 5, Sec. 4.3) measures inversion of synthetically generated images, which differs from the inpainting setting; a convergence/quality analysis directly on the inpainting objective would be more convincing.

Minor presentation issues: the project website URL appears empty in the abstract, and some equations/formulas appear to contain raw LaTeX artifacts; Table 9 in the supplement shows non-monotonic behavior across iterations (10 iterations gives the best FID and IR at 200 NFE) that deserves discussion.

Reproducibility depends on VLM-generated prompts (Claude Sonnet 4.5) for FFHQ/DIV2K, introducing a stochastic, non-trivially-reproducible component into the evaluation pipeline, although the exact prompting templates are provided.
